most dell systems have their usb-c/tb3 video outputs wired to the intel gpu. only a small number of systems have them wired to the nvidia gpu or offer a bios option to allow you to choose which gpu controls the outputs. the latter capability is something that i’ve only seen within dell systems on the precision 7000 series systems, and more recently on the xps 17 9700/precision 5750 but only when ordered with an rtx gpu. it’s likely that your system has that output wired to the intel gpu without the necessary bios option to change it because it doesn’t have the necessary motherboard design to offer that type of flexibility. and the intel gpus built into core 9th gen cpus only supports displayport 1.2/hbr2, which is only enough bandwidth for 4k 60 hz. a tb3 connection can carry dual dp 1.2 source interfaces from the gpu, but intel gpus do not support aggregating multiple interfaces to drive a single display. so tb3 could allow you to drive dual 4k 60 hz, but not single 4k 120 hz even though those two setups require the same total bandwidth. disabling optimus in your case would simply disable the nvidia gpu. it would not remove the intel gpu from the video path, since that isn’t possible on your system’s design, at least for its usb-c/tb3 port. all that said, if nvidia control panel indicates that the mdp output is directly controlled by the nvidia gpu, then that would be the right choice, since that output might support dp 1.4/hbr3. if the port stops working when playing games and gets overheated, it sounds like you have a hardware issue though.

the answer to the gpu question is a bit more complicated on both sides.the d6000 uses displaylink. due to a windows limitation, displays attached via displaylink can only use gpu acceleration from the system's primary gpu. on a system with both an intel and nvidia gpu enabled, that will be the intel gpu. so you'd never get the benefit of the nvidia gpu. but it's worse than that. displaylink technology itself imposes some significant drawbacks for certain use cases, including and especially gaming. i wrote about those in detail in this thread, specifically the post marked as the answer. the bottom line is that displaylink performance is even worse than a display that was driven "normally" by the intel gpu, even if it didn't have access to the nvidia gpu.the wd19 family taps into the system's native gpu outputs available on usb-c or thunderbolt 3. as a result, none of the penalties of displaylink apply, and displays attached to that dock will have access to the nvidia gpu just as if you attached a display directly to the system. however, on most display outputs of systems -- and all usb-c/t3 outputs that i've seen on dell systems thus far -- the intel gpu still has direct control of the output itself. that means that the nvidia gpu when needed steps in as a render-only device to do the heavy lifting and then passes completed video frames to the intel gpu for output to the attached displays. this technology is called nvidia optimus. the vast majority of laptops are set up this way because by preventing the nvidia gpu from having direct control of display outputs, it can be completely disabled when it's not needed, which saves battery life. if the nvidia gpu had direct control of outputs, then it would need to be active whenever a display was attached, even if nothing graphics-intensive was going on. the catch is that there are certain technologies that the intel gpu doesn't support passing through and/or that nvidia gpus can only use if they have direct control of the display output. these include vr, g-sync, adaptive v-sync, stereoscopic 3d, and a few others. however, once again that isn't a limitation of the dock. it's simply an aspect of the system design. certain systems have at least some display outputs directly wired to the nvidia gpu instead specifically to make it possible to use those technologies i just listed, but i don't know if the 5590 is set up that way, and once again on every dell system i've seen, the usb-c/tb3 ports are always wired to the intel gpu (except the precision 7000 series models where a bios option allows you to choose which gpu has control of the display outputs).

happy to help! in terms of vr, be aware of a potential pitfall there. on the gaming systems that have a display output wired to the discrete gpu, it's typically the hdmi output, because the initial wave of vr headsets used hdmi. some still do. however, the new oculus rift s switched over to displayport. displayport video output can be achieved from a usb-c port that supports video output by using a usb-c to displayport dongle. however, on every dell system i'm aware of that has a usb-c port that supports video output, the usb-c port's video interface is wired to the intel gpu. the only exceptions i know of are the precision 7000 series models from the xx20 onward, which have a bios option that allows you to choose which gpu controls the display outputs. they achieve that with a more complex and expensive motherboard design, but i haven't seen that implemented elsewhere.so if you're trying for vr, you might have to give some thought to which vr headset you want to use, because if you have a system where only the hdmi output is wired to the discrete gpu, then you can't use a displayport-based vr headset. there are displayport to hdmi adapters, but they don't work in that direction. they can only convert a displayport source to an hdmi signal, not the other way around. there's also a new standard called virtuallink that is backed by all major vr headset and gpu manufacturers that is basically a new way to configure a usb-c interface to carry enough power, video, and data to run an entire vr headset from a single cable. it's expected to be used on future vr headsets. i may be wrong here, but i don't think it will be possible to retrofit virtuallink support to existing systems because virtuallink basically involves running usb 3.0 traffic over pins on the usb-c connector that the current spec reserves for usb 2.0 (in order to increase available video bandwidth by reconfiguring the typical usb 3.0 pins for video). that said, i don't know of any while i'm not familiar with your particular model i suspect that it has a lithium polymer battery like my vostro 5502. lipo batteries do not like to be deep discharged. i had two deep discharge events (down to near 0% charge) with my vostro and each time the capacity decreased slightly. it's now down to 92.2%. the solution is to not let the battery drop to below 30% capacity. when you hit 30%, plug it in. another problem with deep discharging is that the battery will start to puff. flammable hydrogen gas will start to build up inside the battery casing and the battery will start to grow larger. this is why you hear about people having touchpad and keyboard problems. the battery expands and starts pressing on things it should not be pressing on. yes, i said flammable. look up lipo fire on youtube. i've been playing with lipo batteries since 2009 for model airplane use. i learned early on not to deep discharge lipo's. i have some in service that are over 7 years old and they still hold a good charge. i have gotten good at timing flights and tend to land with the batteries at ~50% capacity. another top tip is if you intend to let your laptop sit unused for more than two weeks perform a storage charge. a storage charge is simply charge or discharge the battery to ~60%. it will then be safe to leave the laptop unused for months. never leave a lipo battery unused for long periods of time fully charged, it will ultimately reduce the fully charged capacity. all of my fancy lipo chargers have a storage charge function to automate this process. this function will either charge of discharge the battery to 60% automatically. in summary, do not discharge your laptop below 30% and you should no longer see the decrease in fully charged capacity assuming that your battery is not already too far gone. dell should be telling us about this but they are in the business of selling replacement laptops and laptop batteries.

i know it would work with them in the sense that you can send a picture to them, but my understanding is that you wouldn't be able to use the actual g-sync feature with them. the dell d6000 uses displaylink (not to be confused with displayport), and due to a windows limitation, that means that on systems with both intel and nvidia gpus active, you can't even use the nvidia gpu's graphical acceleration horsepower, because displaylink will only allow you to use the primary gpu, which in dual gpu systems will be the intel gpu. and g-sync requires not only that the nvidia gpu be used, but that it have direct control of the display output connector. on most laptops, the nvidia gpu doesn't have direct control of any outputs and instead works through nvidia optimus as a render-only device that passes completed video frames to the intel gpu, which is directly connected to the display outputs. but displaylink in particular is an "indirect display" technology that involves compressing rendered video and transmitting it as regular usb data. that's how the d6000 and other displaylink-based adapters and docks can support plugging into a system over usb-a, which has no native video output support. so in that case, neither of the system's gpus would have direct control of the display output connector.if you're claiming that the d6000 supports g-sync displays and that g-sync can actually be enabled for such displays when connected through the d6000, what is your source for that?

you can install drivers downloaded directly from nvidia onto your laptop, but enabling stereoscopic 3d requires that the nvidia gpu be directly wired to the display you want to use, and that might not be the case in your system. in most laptops with both integrated (intel) and discrete gpus, the built-in display is still wired to the integrated gpu, and in many cases most or even all external display outputs are also wired to the integrated gpu. in those cases, when the discrete gpu's extra performance is needed, it acts as a render-only device that passes completed video frames to the integrated gpu for output to the display(s). for nvidia, this technology is called optimus. the benefit of this design is that when the discrete gpu's performance is not needed, it can be completely disabled, which saves battery life, but the downside is that certain technologies that the intel gpu does not support passing through and/or that are proprietary to nvidia and therefore always require the nvidia gpu to have direct control of the display output aren't available. those technologies include stereoscopic 3d, g-sync, vr, and some others.in nvidia control panel, if you check either the physx or multi-display area, i believe one of those areas shows a diagram indicating which displays are wired to which gpu. that might be useful.

ok first of all, ahci and uefi are not "opposites". they're completely different things that are configured in completely different sections of the bios setup. uefi is a boot type, and the other boot type option is legacy (aka bios). ahci is a storage interface operation mode, and the other option there is raid. despite the "sata operation" setting name, it also affects how the system treats nvme ssds. but the point is that you can can have a system that boots in uefi mode and runs its storage interface in ahci mode -- or a system that boots in uefi mode and runs its storage interface in raid mode, which is the factory default configuration.the reason you're having an issue is that as you should have been warned when you tried to change the raid setting to ahci, that setting isn't meant to be changed on an installed os. it's designed to be changed before you reinstall an os. the reason is that if windows is installed while the system is in raid mode, then it will configure itself to load the intel rapid storage driver at boot in order to see the storage device. if you then reconfigure the system to run in ahci mode, then windows won't be configured to load the correct driver at boot anymore, so it will fail. in order to reduce boot time, there are certain devices and drivers where windows does not dynamically adjust based on the installed hardware and its configuration. instead, it just stores assumptions about how the hardware will be configured, so if you change the hardware configuration, then those assumptions are invalid and windows doesn't start. the same would occur if you had installed windows while in ahci mode and later decided to switch to raid.there are some manual hoops you can jump through in order to switch an existing windows installation over to ahci mode. they involve booting in safe mode at some point and possibly some other tasks. i haven't looked into them in detail. but if you were to perform multiple benchmarks in both raid mode and ahci mode, i doubt you'd see much of a consistent performance difference, if any at all. so if you're not all that techy, you might want to just leave this one alone.

g-sync only works over displayport (and usb-c, which uses displayport signaling for video), but it also requires that the display output be wired directly to the nvidia gpu. many laptops have most or all outputs wired to the intel gpu, with the nvidia gpu operating as a render-only device through a technology called nvidia optimus. that has battery life advantages since it allows the nvidia gpu to be completely disabled when its horsepower isn't needed, but it prevents g-sync from being used (as well as vr, adaptive v-sync, stereoscopic 3d, and some other technologies).so before you buy your display, check whether either the usb-c or mini-displayport output is wired to the nvidia gpu. to do that, connect a display to the output, then go to nvidia control panel and open the physx configuration section, which will include a diagram showing which gpu controls each active display. if the display you connected as a test shows as being wired to the intel gpu, you won't be able to use g-sync through that output. to my knowledge, all current dell systems have their usb-c/tb3 ports wired to the intel gpu, except precision 7000 series systems that have a bios option allowing you to choose which gpu controls the display outputs -- but that capability doesn't seem to be implemented elsewhere. the mini-displayport output is your best bet here, because some alienware and inspiron gaming systems do have at least one display output wired to the discrete gpu specifically to support technologies like vr, g-sync, etc.in terms of cables, i'm pretty sure 1440p 165 hz will run over a regular displayport 1.2 interface, in which case you wouldn't need anything special because displayport 1.2 has been around for a long time, so you'd need a truly ancient displayport cable for it not to support at least 1.2.
